description: "The last lecture of CS229: the helicopter diagnostics restated in reinforcement-learning notation, then direct policy search, which skips the value function and tunes a stochastic policy by gradient ascent on its expected payoff. The REINFORCE update, a derivation that its average is exactly that gradient, why its noise makes it slow and how weighting each action only by later rewards and subtracting a baseline cut that noise without changing the average, why policy search copes with partial observability, and when a policy is simpler to learn than a value function."

::: {.lecture-video lecture="20"}
:::

*Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — [CS229](https://cs229.stanford.edu/), Stanford
University, Autumn 2018.*

Every reinforcement-learning method in the course so far has been indirect: estimate the
value function, then read the policy off it with an argmax. The last lecture introduces
the other family. *Direct policy search* writes the policy down as a parametrised function,
the way logistic regression writes down a hypothesis, and tunes its parameters by
gradient ascent on the expected payoff, never computing a value function at all. The
algorithm Ng derives, REINFORCE, gets an unbiased estimate of that gradient from a single
run of the system. Unbiased is not the same as useful: the estimate is so noisy that
REINFORCE is notoriously slow, and part of that noise comes from terms that average to
zero and can be dropped. Before any of that, Ng finishes a promise from lecture 12 and
restates the helicopter diagnostics in the notation the course has since introduced.

## Debugging the helicopter, in RL notation {#sec-ps-debug}

[4:05]{.t} Lecture 12 walked through the diagnostics for Ng's autonomous helicopter before
the course had any reinforcement learning to describe them with (@sec-dbg-helicopter). The
setup is now familiar. Build a simulator, a learned model $s_{t+1} = A s_t + B a_t$ or
something richer, as in @sec-cmdp-model. Choose a reward function, such as the negative
squared distance from where the helicopter should be. Run a reinforcement-learning
algorithm on the finite-horizon problem to get a policy $\pi_{\text{RL}}$ that maximises
$\mathbb{E}[R(s_0) + \dots + R(s_T)]$ in the simulator. The first time, the controller flies
much worse than the human pilot, and there are three things to try: improve the simulator,
change the reward, or improve the RL algorithm. Ng is concrete about the last one. It means
changing the discretization of a continuous state, or replacing the linear function
approximator in fitted value iteration with a richer one such as a neural network.

The diagnostics are those of lecture 12 with the sign turned round, since the algorithm now
maximises a payoff rather than minimising a cost. If $\pi_{\text{RL}}$ flies well in
simulation and badly in reality, the simulator is at fault. Otherwise, [8:28]{.t} record the
human pilot's flight and score it with the same reward. If the human's payoff is higher,
the algorithm failed to maximise the sum of rewards, because here is a policy that does
better. If the algorithm's payoff is higher and it still flies worse, maximising this
reward is not the same as flying well, and the reward is what needs work.

[13:12]{.t} A student asks whether the tests have an order. Ng checks the simulator first
and turns to the other two only once it seems adequate. He also qualifies the whole
procedure: the diagnostics look like a rigid decision rule, but in practice the answers are
graded. The simulator is "kind of good", the human beats the algorithm by a little, and the
team looks at all three pieces of evidence together and decides where the next month goes.
What he insists on is that the bottleneck moves as the project progresses, so the
diagnostics are re-run after each round of work rather than once, and teams that
prioritise this way move faster than teams that go by gut feel.

## Searching for the policy directly {#sec-ps-direct}

[17:01]{.t} Ng shows one more example of the indirect route first. Zico Kolter's quadruped
crossing rough terrain relied on an approximate value function that scored, for a given
height map of the terrain, how good each position of the robot was; the robot moved towards
higher value. That is value iteration's way of thinking: learn $V^*$, or an approximation
to it, then act greedily with
$\pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P_{sa}}[V^*(s')]$ (@sec-vi-readout and
@sec-cmdp-policy).

[18:25]{.t} *Direct policy search* goes straight for the policy, with no value function in
between. Its first step is the same as the first step of supervised learning. When
logistic regression was introduced, Ng recalls, the form $h_\theta(x) = g(\theta^\top x)$
was pulled out of a hat (@sec-logistic-model), and the learning algorithm's job was then to
find the best $\theta$ within that form. Policy search likewise starts by choosing a class
of policies, parametrised by $\theta$, and its job is to find the best member of the class.

The running example is the inverted pendulum, a pole on a hinge atop a cart, with two
actions: accelerate left or accelerate right. The state is

$$
s = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x \\ \dot x \\ \phi \\ \dot\phi \end{bmatrix},
$$

the cart's position and velocity and the pole's angle and angular velocity, with a 1 for an
intercept. The angle is $\phi$ rather than the usual $\theta$, which is about to be taken
by the parameters.

## Stochastic policies {#sec-ps-stochastic}

[22:51]{.t} The policies of lectures 16 to 19 were deterministic, a map from states to
actions. Policy search uses a *stochastic policy*, a function $\pi(s, a)$ giving the
probability of taking action $a$ in state $s$:

$$
\pi(s, a) \ge 0, \qquad \sum_a \pi(s, a) = 1 \quad \text{for every } s .
$$

On every step the agent draws its action from $\pi(s, \cdot)$. [24:38]{.t} For the pendulum,
Ng's choice is logistic:

$$
\pi_\theta(s, \text{right}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^\top s}}, \qquad
\pi_\theta(s, \text{left}) = 1 - \pi_\theta(s, \text{right}) .
$$ {#eq-ps-logistic-policy}

[25:47]{.t} To see that this can express sensible behaviour, take
$\theta = (0, 0, 0, 1, 0)$. Then $\theta^\top s = \phi$, and the probability of accelerating
right is $1/(1 + e^{-\phi})$: the further the pole leans to the right, the likelier the cart
is to accelerate right and get back under it. This ignores where the cart is, and a cart
that keeps chasing the pole will run off the end of its track. [27:18]{.t} With
$\theta = (0, -0.5, 0, 1, 0)$ the position enters with a negative weight, so the further
right the cart already is, the less likely it is to accelerate further right. The general
problem is to find the five numbers that trade off position, velocity, angle and angular
velocity best, and that is what the algorithm will do.

@fig-ps-policy plots these policies. One thing the board example hides is scale. With a
weight of 1 on an angle measured in radians, a pole tilted half a radian, nearly
thirty degrees, still gets accelerated the right way only 62 % of the time: the policy is
close to a coin flip over every angle a balancing controller would see. The signs in
$\theta$ say which way to lean; the magnitude says how decisively, and a weight of 10
turns the same policy into almost a step. The learning algorithm has to find both.

![Probability of accelerating right against the pole angle, for the logistic policy @eq-ps-logistic-policy. Purple: Ng's weight of 1 on the angle; teal: the same direction scaled by ten. Solid: the cart at $x = 0$; dashed: the cart at $x = 1$ with a weight of $-0.5$ times the angle weight on position, which shifts each curve right. Computed in `figures/20-policy-search/make_diagrams.py`.](../figures/20-policy-search/diagram_policy.svg){#fig-ps-policy}

[49:04]{.t} Later, answering a question, Ng gives the reason for the switch to stochastic
policies. A deterministic policy over two actions is a step function of $\theta$, either
left or right, and there is no derivative to follow. Probabilities move smoothly with
$\theta$, so the expected payoff becomes differentiable and gradient ascent applies.

## The objective {#sec-ps-objective}

[29:03]{.t} The goal is to choose $\theta$ to maximise the expected payoff when the policy
is run:

$$
\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}\left[R(s_0, a_0) + R(s_1, a_1) + \dots + R(s_T, a_T) \,\middle|\, \pi_\theta\right],
$$ {#eq-ps-objective}

in the finite-horizon setting of @sec-lqr-finite-horizon, with rewards that may depend on the
action as in @sec-lqr-state-action. For the pendulum the reward might be $-1$ whenever the
pole falls over and 0 otherwise.

[30:15]{.t} One difference from value iteration is easy to miss. $V^*$ gives the optimal
policy for every starting state at once, so a single $\pi^*$ is simultaneously best from
wherever the system begins. Policy search optimises from one fixed initial state $s_0$, or
one fixed distribution over initial states, and the policy it finds is best for that start.
A policy class too small to contain $\pi^*$ forces a trade-off between states, and the
initial distribution decides which states the trade-off favours.

## REINFORCE {#sec-ps-reinforce}

[32:02]{.t} To keep the board manageable, Ng sets $T = 1$: two states and two actions. The
expectation in @eq-ps-objective is then a sum over every state-action sequence, weighted by
its probability:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{payoff}] = \sum_{s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1}
P(s_0)\, \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\, P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)\, \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)
\left[R(s_0, a_0) + R(s_1, a_1)\right].
$$ {#eq-ps-expectation}

The initial distribution $P(s_0)$ and the transition probabilities $P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)$ do not
depend on $\theta$; only the two policy factors do. Everything below carries over to longer
horizons with longer products and sums.

[34:58]{.t} The algorithm that climbs this objective is called REINFORCE, after
Williams' 1992 paper
([Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00992696)).
Ng presents its core and notes that the original has a few further refinements, one of
which comes up below. Each iteration does three things:

1. Run the system for $T$ steps under the current policy, sampling each action from
   $\pi_\theta$, to get a sequence $s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \dots, s_T, a_T$.
2. Compute the payoff, the sum of the rewards along it.
3. Update
   $$
   \theta := \theta + \alpha \left[\sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_t, a_t)}{\pi_\theta(s_t, a_t)}\right] \times \text{payoff}.
   $$ {#eq-ps-reinforce}

[37:48]{.t} Each update is random, because it depends on which states the system happened
to visit and which actions the policy happened to draw. Ng's picture is the one he drew for
stochastic gradient descent on linear regression (@sec-sgd): batch gradient descent heads
straight for the optimum, while the stochastic version takes a jittery path that heads the
right way on average. The claim is that REINFORCE is stochastic gradient *ascent* on the
expected payoff: the expected value of the bracketed update is exactly the gradient of
@eq-ps-expectation.

## Why the update follows the gradient {#sec-ps-gradient}

[40:05]{.t} The proof is three lines of calculus. Differentiate @eq-ps-expectation. Inside
the sum only the two $\pi_\theta$ factors depend on $\theta$, so the product rule gives two
terms:

$$
\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[\text{payoff}] = \sum_{s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1}
P(s_0)\, P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)
\left[\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\, \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1) + \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\, \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)\right]
\times \text{payoff}.
$$

[43:58]{.t} Now multiply and divide the first term by $\pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)$ and the second by
$\pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)$. Both terms then contain the full product
$P(s_0)\,\pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)\,P_{s_0 a_0}(s_1)\,\pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)$, which is the
probability of the whole sequence, and it factors out:

$$
\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[\text{payoff}] = \sum_{s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1}
P(s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1)
\left[\frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)}{\pi_\theta(s_0, a_0)} + \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)}{\pi_\theta(s_1, a_1)}\right]
\times \text{payoff}.
$$ {#eq-ps-gradient}

That is a probability-weighted sum over sequences of exactly the quantity REINFORCE adds to
$\theta$ in @eq-ps-reinforce, so it is the expected value of that update. [48:03]{.t} With a
small learning rate, many updates average out and the parameters drift along the gradient
of the expected payoff. Each ratio $\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta / \pi_\theta$ is
$\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta$, the *score* of the action, which is the form the update is
usually written in today. For the logistic policy @eq-ps-logistic-policy it is the familiar
$(\mathbb{1}\{a = \text{right}\} - \pi_\theta(s, \text{right}))\, s$, the same expression as
the logistic-regression gradient (@sec-logistic-mle), now weighted by the payoff instead of
the label error.

The generator for this chapter checks @eq-ps-gradient by two routes on a small
pole-balancing problem described below. It enumerates every two-step trajectory to compute
the expected REINFORCE update exactly, differentiates the expected payoff numerically
through a dynamic programme, and finds the two agree to $10^{-8}$ at twenty random settings
of $\theta$.

[48:36]{.t} A student asks whether the derivation depends on the logistic form. It does not.
Nothing in it used anything about $\pi_\theta$ except that it is the probability of the
action and that it is differentiable in $\theta$. A softmax over many actions works, and so
does a logistic function of elaborate features of the state. [50:48]{.t} The same holds for
continuous actions, which policy search handles without discretizing. If the action is a
real number, the force on the cart or a car's steering angle, a natural policy is
$a = \theta^\top s + \varepsilon$ with Gaussian $\varepsilon$; $\pi_\theta(s, a)$ becomes a
Gaussian density, and the same update applies with the density in place of the probability.

[49:40]{.t} Another student asks why not skip all this and train the helicopter by
supervised learning on a human pilot's stick inputs, learning the map from state to the
pilot's action. Ng thinks that might fly a helicopter slowly without crashing it, but not
well. Learning from rewards is what let the controller fly some manoeuvres better than the
human pilots did, and imitation gives the controller no signal for doing better than the teacher it
copies.

## Why REINFORCE is slow, and what helps {#sec-ps-variance}

[58:14]{.t} Ng is blunt about the cost. The expected update is exactly right, but each
individual update is very noisy, so REINFORCE needs a small learning rate and a very large
number of iterations. Papers that use it routinely report millions of them.

Part of that noise is self-inflicted, and the lecture's form of the update shows where.
@eq-ps-reinforce multiplies the score of *every* action by the *whole* payoff, including
rewards collected before the action was taken. The action at step $t$ cannot have affected
those, and the corresponding terms average to zero. The reason is an identity that holds in
every state:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta(s, \cdot)}\left[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s, a)\right]
= \sum_a \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s, a) = \nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(s, a) = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0 .
$$

A reward from before step $t$ is fixed by the time $a_t$ is drawn, so its product with the
score of $a_t$ has mean zero. Those terms contribute nothing to the expected update and add
variance to every individual one. Dropping them gives the update usually written for
REINFORCE, with each action weighted only by the rewards that follow it:

$$
\theta := \theta + \alpha \sum_{t=0}^{T} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(s_t, a_t)
\left(\sum_{\tau = t}^{T} R(s_\tau, a_\tau) - b_t\right).
$$ {#eq-ps-reinforce-baseline}

The same identity licenses $b_t$, a *baseline*: any quantity that does not depend on the
action $a_t$ can be subtracted from the weight without changing the expected update. A good
choice is the expected reward-to-go from step $t$, which turns the weight into a measure of
whether the run went better or worse than usual from that point. That is one of the
refinements in Williams' original algorithm, whose update is written with a reinforcement
baseline from the start.

The generator checks all three versions on a toy that keeps every expectation computable.
The pole's tilt is an integer from $-2$ to $2$, and it falls, ending the reward, if it
leaves that range. Gravity pushes a tilted pole further over with probability one half;
an upright pole wobbles either way with probability a quarter each. Accelerating
corrects the tilt by one step with probability 0.6. The reward is 1 for every step the pole
is up, over 20 transitions, and the policy is
$\pi_\theta(s, \text{right}) = 1/(1 + e^{-(\theta_0 + \theta_1 s)})$. At $\theta = 0$, the
coin-flip policy, the expected payoff is 5.25 and the best deterministic policy gets
13.50. Averaged over 20,000 runs, all three estimators agree with the numerically
differentiated gradient, $\partial J / \partial \theta_1 = 2.34$, within their standard
errors. Their variances do not agree. On $\theta_1$, the lecture's version has variance 174,
the rewards-that-follow version 51, and with the baseline 19: nine times less noise for the
same expected step.

![Exact expected payoff of the current policy during REINFORCE on the toy balancing problem, averaged over 20 runs, for the lecture's update @eq-ps-reinforce (whole payoff), @eq-ps-reinforce-baseline with $b_t = 0$ (rewards that follow), and @eq-ps-reinforce-baseline with $b_t$ the expected reward-to-go. Dashed: the best deterministic policy. Computed in `figures/20-policy-search/make_diagrams.py`.](../figures/20-policy-search/diagram_learning.svg){#fig-ps-learning}

@fig-ps-learning shows what that buys. At step size $\alpha = 0.01$ all three approach the
optimum, but the lecture's version needs about 290 updates for its average run to reach
90 % of the best payoff, against 130 and 110 for the other two. At $\alpha = 0.03$ the
lower-variance versions get there in about 100 and 40 updates. The lecture's version does
not get there at all on average: after 500 updates, 5 of its 20 runs are still below 90 %
of the best payoff. Inspecting them shows how it fails. A single large, noisy step throws
the intercept $\theta_0$ far from zero, the policy then pushes the same way in almost every
state, and with the sigmoid saturated the scores, and so the further updates, are tiny. A
larger step size is not available to an estimator this noisy, which is Ng's point about
small learning rates, and removing terms that average to zero is the cheapest way to make
it available.

## Partial observability {#sec-ps-pomdp}

[52:24]{.t} Ng names two situations in which direct policy search is the better choice. The
first is a *partially observable* MDP, or POMDP. Suppose the pendulum has a position sensor
and an angle sensor but nothing that measures velocities, and both sensors are noisy. On
each step the agent sees not the state but an observation

$$
y = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ \phi \end{bmatrix} + \text{noise},
$$

two noisy readings of four state variables, and it still has to choose an action.

Value-function methods are stuck here. [55:34]{.t} Even with $V^*$ and $\pi^*$ in hand, the
policy $\pi^*(s)$ needs the state, which the agent does not have. There is a large academic
literature that extends value-based methods to POMDPs, but in Ng's assessment those
algorithms are very complicated and are not widely used in production. Policy search needs
no extension. Define the policy on what the agent can see,

$$
\pi_\theta(y, \text{right}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^\top y}},
$$

and REINFORCE runs unchanged: nothing in @eq-ps-gradient required the policy's input to be
the state, only that the action's probability be a differentiable function of $\theta$. The
policy may not be as good as one that sees the state, but the algorithm finds the best one
of this form.

[57:00]{.t} The input can be any features of the history, not just the current reading.
A common design is to run a state estimator, such as a Kalman filter, over all the
measurements so far, which produces an estimate of the full state vector including the
velocities, and feed that estimate to the policy as its features.

## Policy or value function? {#sec-ps-choose}

[58:59]{.t} The second consideration is which object is simpler. Ng distinguishes
*low-level control* tasks, the ones a skilled human does by feel with a joystick in a
fraction of a second: hovering a helicopter, balancing an inverted pendulum, keeping a car
in its lane on a straight road. For those a simple function of the state, often close to
linear, is a good policy, so a small policy class contains a good answer, and direct policy
search is promising. Chess and Go are the opposite: a good move depends on reasoning several
steps ahead, no simple function of the board position plays well, and value-function
approximation is the more promising route. Driving sits on both sides. Staying in the lane
is low-level control; planning to overtake one car before a truck arrives in that lane is
multi-step reasoning.

[1:02:01]{.t} The helicopter went through both phases. Ng's first controllers, including the
one in the inverted-flight video at the start of the lecture, came from a direct policy
search algorithm, a relative of REINFORCE rather than REINFORCE itself. More complicated
manoeuvres called for methods closer to value-function approximation. The two families
combine, too: Ng cites [AlphaGo](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16961), which trained a
policy network and a value network and used both in its search.

[1:03:20]{.t} The course closes with where reinforcement learning was being applied in 2018.
Game playing is the visible case, but Ng expects robotics to matter most, and mentions
large-machine control in industry, factory optimisation, sequential medical decisions in
which each test result decides the next step, and the execution of large stock trades in
pieces small enough not to move the price. The common thread is the one the whole
reinforcement-learning unit has been about: a sequence of decisions whose payoff arrives
only over time.

::: {.callout-note title="In the official notes"}
The 2018 notes for this part of the course, cs229-notes12, cover MDPs, value and policy
iteration and continuous-state MDPs, and end before policy search. The lecture is the
source for REINFORCE here; Williams' 1992 paper has the general form, including the
baseline.
:::
